Hi, yeah, thanks for seeing me. Um, so I came in because... well, I drive a taxi. It's how I make my money right now since I finished high school, and I'm trying to study on the side, but things have just gotten really, really bad lately.

Yeah. Yeah, exactly. It's... it's not just a quick walk-around like they taught us in training. It's this whole... process. And it has to be perfect. 

Like, before I can even take a single ride, before I even turn the key in the ignition, I have to go around the car. And I check the tires, right? I have to physically press on each one, check the tread, make sure there's no nails. Then the lights. Headlights, brights, blinkers, brake lights, reverse lights. Then the doors—I have to open and slam each one to make sure it latches properly. Then I check the meter, make sure it's zeroed out, make sure the paper roll is full. Then the paperwork in the glovebox, the registration, the insurance. 

And I do it over and over. I'll finish the loop, and my brain will just be like, "Did you really check the back left door? Are you sure?" And so I have to do the whole thing again. Sometimes... sometimes I even take pictures with my phone. Like, I'll take a picture of the tire, or a video of me pulling on the door handle, just so I have proof. But even then, if I'm looking at the video and it just doesn't... feel right, you know? Like if I didn't pull the handle hard enough in the video, or if the lighting is weird and I can't clearly see the tire tread... I have to delete the video and start the entire check all over again from the beginning. 

And I'll be doing this, just looping around the cab, and there will literally be passengers standing on the curb waiting for me. Like, I can see them looking at me, getting annoyed, checking their phones. And I'm already late, I'm already behind schedule, dispatch is probably going to yell at me again, but I just... I can't stop. I can't get in the car and drive until the check feels exactly right, no matter how many times I have to do it or who's watching me. It's like I'm trapped in my own parking space.

Oh, completely. I definitely do not want them there. Honestly, that's the whole reason I came in to see you in the first place. I never sit down and try to conjure this stuff up. It just... it ambushes me.

Yeah. Yeah, exactly, 100%. That's... that's the whole reason I do it. Like I was explaining earlier with my whole routine... before I can even take a single ride, I keep going around the car, checking the tires, the lights, the doors, the meter, the paperwork, just over and over again. I'm doing all of that specifically because I feel like if I don't, it's an absolute guarantee that something terrible is going to happen. 

I mean, think about it from my perspective. If I don't do the loop, if I don't physically press on the tread and take those pictures of the tires to prove there's no nail, I'll just be picturing a blowout on the interstate the entire time I'm driving. Or the doors—if I don't slam them and get it on video to prove they latched, I'll start thinking a passenger is going to lean against the door and just fall out into moving traffic. And the paperwork, too... if I don't check the glovebox, I'll be convinced I'm going to get pulled over, get a massive ticket, and get fired, which ruins my chances of ever getting my CDL. 

So, yeah, it's all about trying to stop those disasters. That's why, even when there are passengers literally standing right there on the curb, looking at their watches and getting visibly angry with me, and even when I know I'm already late and dispatch is going to chew me out, I still have to keep checking. I can't just get in and drive. If I take a picture or a video and it doesn't feel exactly right, I have to delete it and restart the whole check from the very beginning. Because if I just drove off without being completely, one-hundred-percent sure that I prevented every possible bad thing... the guilt would just eat me alive. I feel like I'm the only one standing between a normal shift and a complete catastrophe, you know? So I just keep checking.

I just can't turn it off. It just forces its way in.\n\nDoctor: Are you doing the safety checks to prevent something bad from happening?\n\nPatient: Yeah. Yeah, exactly, 100%. Yeah, I do... for a minute, anyway. It's like... okay, like I was telling you a second ago about my routine. Before I can even take a single ride, I have to keep going around the car, right? It's just that I have to go through hell, piss off my passengers, and ruin my schedule just to get that tiny little window of relief, you know? And then as soon as I drop that fare off, the whole thing just starts all over again.

Zero choice. None at all. It's not like I'm just deciding to be overly thorough, you know? It's like... it's like my brain has a gun to my head.

What if there was a nail you missed? What if it blows out on the highway?\" \n\nSo it's definitely coming from inside my own skull, which honestly almost makes it worse, if I'm being real with you. Because it's like... why am I doing this to myself? Why can't I just be a normal nineteen-year-old and drive the cab and go home and study without my own mind sabotaging my entire day? It's just me in there, but it's like this version of me that just absolutely refuses to let anything go, no matter how much I try to tell myself everything is fine.\n\nDoctor: Are these thoughts and worries affecting your relationships with friends or family, or are you able to keep them separate?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, it's... it's really bleeding into everything. I mean, my relationships are definitely taking a hit, but it's not just that, it's my whole life. Like, my friends, they used to call me to hang out on weekends, or even just grab a burger after a shift, but lately I just... I barely see them anymore. I mean, I can't. Half the time I'm so far behind on my work schedule because of all the time I spend checking the car, or I'm just completely exhausted from dealing with it all day. \n\nAnd work... man, work is getting bad. I've actually lost rides because I'm just standing there in the lot staring at the tires or the headlights, and I've gotten warnings from dispatch because I can't get on the road on time. They're like, \"Where are you? Your shift started twenty minutes ago,\" and I'm just... I'm stuck. I can't leave the lot until I feel like I've checked it enough. And then, because my work takes so long, I'm trying to catch up all day, which means I have zero energy left when I get home. \n\nI'm supposed to be studying for my CDL—my commercial driver's license—so I can maybe get a better job, drive trucks or something, you know? Something that pays more than driving a cab around the city. But my studying just keeps getting pushed back and pushed back. I'll sit down with the manual, and my brain is still just screaming about whether I locked the cab doors properly or if the parking brake was pulled up all the way, and I end up reading the same paragraph like five times without absorbing a single word. So much of my day just gets completely eaten up by this... this routine, or whatever you want to call it. So, yeah, it's definitely not just something I can keep separate. It's kind of ruining my friendships, my job, my studying... pretty much everything.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you have to perform the safety check in a specific way or a certain number of times to try to stop these worrying thoughts?\n\nPatient: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. It's... it's not just a quick walk-around like they taught us in training. It's this whole... process. And it has to be perfect. \n\nLike, before I can even take a single ride, before I even turn the key in the ignition, I have to go around the car. And I check the tires, right? I have to physically press on each one, check the tread, make sure there's no nails. Then the lights. Headlights, brights, blinkers, brake lights, reverse lights. Then the doors—I have to open and slam each one to make sure it latches properly. Then I check the meter, make sure it's zeroed out, make sure the paper roll is full. Then the paperwork in the glovebox, the registration, the insurance. \n\nAnd I do it over and over. I'll finish the loop, and my brain will just be like, \"Did you really check the back left door? Are you sure?\" And so I have to do the whole thing again. Sometimes... sometimes I even take pictures with my phone. Like, I'll take a picture of the tire, or a video of me pulling on the door handle, just so I have proof. But even then, if I'm looking at the video and it just doesn't... feel right, you know? Like if I didn't pull the handle hard enough in the video, or if the lighting is weird and I can't clearly see the tire tread... I have to delete the video and start the entire check all over again from the beginning. \n\nAnd I'll be doing this, just looping around the cab, and there will literally be passengers standing on the curb waiting for me. Like, I can see them looking at me, getting annoyed, checking their phones. And I'm already late, I'm already behind schedule, dispatch is probably going to yell at me again, but I just... I can't stop. I can't get in the car and drive until the check feels exactly right, no matter how many times I have to do it or who's watching me. It's like I'm trapped in my own parking space.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like these thoughts and behaviors are causing you significant distress or are interfering with your daily life in a major way?\n\nPatient: Yeah, I mean... absolutely. Like I was kind of getting into earlier, it's... it's basically taking over my entire life. The distress is... well, it's overwhelming, honestly. I just feel so stuck. \n\nLike, I mentioned the warnings from dispatch, right? It's not just a quick \"hey, hurry up\" over the radio. I've literally lost rides. Good rides, too, like long airport runs that actually pay well. I'll be stuck in the lot, doing my checking loop for the third or fourth time, trying to get the video of the door handle just right, and dispatch will call my number, and I just have to sit there and listen to another driver take my fare because I can't get on the road on time. That's money right out of my pocket, you know? It's my livelihood. And my boss is starting to look at me like I'm completely unreliable, which just adds to the stress of it all.\n\nAnd then because I'm losing time and money, I'm constantly trying to catch up. So my CDL studying... the thing that's supposed to be my ticket out of driving this cab... it just keeps getting pushed back and pushed back. I'll finally get home, sit at my desk, open the commercial driving manual, but so much of my day has already been eaten up by this... this endless checking routine, that my brain is just completely fried. I'll stare at the page about air brakes or weight limits or whatever, and I'm just exhausted. I can't retain anything. \n\nAnd that totally bleeds into my social life, too. I barely see my friends anymore. They'll text me on a Friday night to hang out, and I just... I can't do it. I'm either still out on the road because I'm behind on my shift from all the checking delays, or I'm at home desperately trying to catch up on the studying I missed, or honestly, I'm just too drained to even pretend to be normal around them. I just make up excuses now. I'll tell them I picked up an extra shift or I'm not feeling well. I can't exactly tell them I spent forty-five minutes kicking a tire, you know? So, yeah, to answer your question, it's a major interference. It really feels like I'm just watching my life pass me by while I'm stuck walking in circles around a taxi.\n\nDoctor: Would you say that these thoughts about missing something on the cab are unwanted and pop into your mind without you intentionally thinking about them?\n\nPatient: Oh, completely. I definitely do not want them there. Honestly, that's the whole reason I came in to see you in the first place. I never sit down and try to conjure this stuff up. It just... it ambushes me. \n\nLike, I'll be driving, right? Just cruising down 4th Avenue, maybe I've got a fare in the back heading to the airport, the radio is on, I'm just looking at the traffic lights. And then, bam. Like, I know I did it, I probably did it five times and have the video on my phone to prove it, but my brain just ignores all that and starts screaming at me anyway. \n\nIt'll just pop in and be like, \"Are you sure the lug nuts were tight? Because if they aren't, the wheel is going to fly off into the crosswalk and somebody could get seriously hurt.\" Or if it's not that, it's about work. It'll tell me that my boss is going to randomly inspect the car, he's going to see I missed a bald spot on the tire or a cracked taillight, and he's going to say I lied on my pre-trip report. \n\nAnd once that thought pops into my head, I just... I can't make it shut up. I try, you know? I try to shake my head, I'll turn the radio up louder, I try to force myself to focus on the road, but it's just playing on a loop, blaring in my mind the entire time I'm driving. And it's the exact same thing when I'm at home. Like I was saying about trying to study for my CDL... I'll be staring right at the manual, trying to memorize weight limits or something, completely trying to focus, and suddenly my brain is just hijacking me with all these scenarios about people getting injured or my boss calling me a liar. I just can't turn it off. It just forces its way in.\n\nDoctor: Are you doing the safety checks to prevent something bad from happening?\n\nPatient: Yeah. Yeah, exactly, 100%. That's... that's the whole reason I do it. Like I was explaining earlier with my whole routine... before I can even take a single ride, I keep going around the car, checking the tires, the lights, the doors, the meter, the paperwork, just over and over again. I'm doing all of that specifically because I feel like if I don't, it's an absolute guarantee that something terrible is going to happen. \n\nI mean, think about it from my perspective. If I don't do the loop, if I don't physically press on the tread and take those pictures of the tires to prove there's no nail, I'll just be picturing a blowout on the interstate the entire time I'm driving. And the paperwork, too... if I don't check the glovebox, I'll be convinced I'm going to get pulled over, get a massive ticket, and get fired, which ruins my chances of ever getting my CDL. \n\nSo, yeah, it's all about trying to stop those disasters. That's why, even when there are passengers literally standing right there on the curb, looking at their watches and getting visibly angry with me, and even when I know I'm already late and dispatch is going to chew me out, I still have to keep checking. I can't just get in and drive. If I take a picture or a video and it doesn't feel exactly right, I have to delete it and restart the whole check from the very beginning. Because if I just drove off without being completely, one-hundred-percent sure that I prevented every possible bad thing... the guilt would just eat me alive. I feel like I'm the only one standing between a normal shift and a complete catastrophe, you know? So I just keep checking.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel less anxious or worried after completing your safety checks?\n\nPatient: Yeah, I do... for a minute, anyway. Checking the tires, the lights, the doors, the meter, the paperwork, just over and over again. And I'm taking those pictures and videos on my phone. The panic just kind of drains out of me, and I can actually breathe for a second. \n\nBut getting to that point is just so exhausting. But I still had to restart the whole check of the doors and the lights and the meter and everything. I couldn't just stop and let him in, because the anxiety would have been unbearable. I had to finish the routine to make the worry stop. \n\nSo, yes, completing it does make me feel less anxious, absolutely. It's the only thing that works. It's just that I have to go through hell, piss off my passengers, and ruin my schedule just to get that tiny little window of relief, you know? And then as soon as I drop that fare off, the whole thing just starts all over again.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you have no choice but to perform these safety checks?\n\nPatient: Zero choice. I'll be staring right at the manual, trying to memorize weight limits or something, completely trying to focus, and suddenly my brain is just hijacking me with all these scenarios about people getting injured or my boss calling me a liar. Honestly, it's... it's the uncertainty. I mean, like I said, logically I know the car is probably fine. I know a tire isn't just going to spontaneously explode if I don't look at it for a fifth time.
